title: Space Complexity & Advanced Complexity Classes
summary: Space complexity (L, NL, PSPACE) and a light touch on randomized complexity — rounding out the complexity landscape beyond P/NP.

slides.markdown:
So far, complexity classes measured **time**. **Space complexity** asks the parallel question: how much **memory** does an algorithm need, as input size grows — separate from how long it takes.

Some algorithms are fast but memory-hungry; others are slow but tiny in memory. Space classes (`L`, `NL`, `PSPACE`) categorize by this second, independent axis.

- `L`/`NL` — extremely tight budgets (logarithmic in input size).
- `PSPACE` — polynomial memory, a much larger budget.
- These interact with, but aren't identical to, the time classes P and NP.

slides.subTitle: L and NL
slides.markdown:
**L** is problems solvable using only **logarithmic** extra memory — `O(log n)` space — regardless of input size. **NL** is the nondeterministic version (a certificate checkable in log space).

Why log space? It's enough to store a handful of pointers into the input (an index into size-`n` array needs `log n` bits) — not enough to copy the input itself.

Graph reachability ("is there a path from `s` to `t`") is the canonical NL-complete problem — checkable with a constant number of node-index pointers.

slides.subTitle: PSPACE
slides.markdown:
**PSPACE** allows **polynomial** memory — `O(n^k)` space, far larger than log space.

A key known fact: `NP ⊆ PSPACE`. A nondeterministic polynomial-time computation can be simulated deterministically using only polynomial space (even at exponential time cost), so everything in NP fits PSPACE's memory budget.

![PSPACE contains NP, which contains P](assets/pspace-np-nesting.svg)

assets.alt: PSPACE contains NP, which contains P

slides.subTitle: Savitch's theorem
slides.markdown:
**Savitch's theorem** shows nondeterminism barely matters for space, unlike time: any problem solvable with `f(n)` space nondeterministically can be solved with `f(n)²` space **deterministically**.

This is surprising — for time, we don't know if P = NP (removing nondeterminism might cost exponentially more). For space, removing nondeterminism costs just a **squaring**.

Consequence: `NPSPACE = PSPACE` — a much cleaner picture than the time-complexity world.

slides.subTitle: Randomized complexity: BPP
slides.markdown:
**BPP** (bounded-error probabilistic polynomial time) is problems solvable in polynomial time by an algorithm allowed to **flip coins**, with a bounded error rate made arbitrarily small by repeating and majority-voting.

Practical randomized algorithms — primality testing, load-balancing, hashing schemes (Area 1 covers these) — live here. It's open whether `BPP = P`, i.e. whether randomness ever gives genuine extra power over determinism.

This is a third axis (randomness), layered on the time/space picture, not a replacement for it.

slides.subTitle: What we actually know
slides.markdown:
The proven containment chain: **L ⊆ NL ⊆ P ⊆ NP ⊆ PSPACE**.

![The proven containment chain from L to PSPACE](assets/complexity-containment-chain.svg)

| Class | Resource bound |
|---|---|
| L / NL | O(log n) space |
| P | polynomial time |
| NP | polynomial time, nondeterministic |
| PSPACE | polynomial space |

Every arrow above is a proven `⊆`. Whether **any** of them is a strict `⊂` (i.e., the classes are actually different) is, almost entirely, still unknown.

assets.alt: The proven containment chain from L to PSPACE

slides.markdown:
We know `L ⊆ NL ⊆ P ⊆ NP ⊆ PSPACE` but can't say whether any containment is *strict*. The gap is a proof-technique problem: known methods (diagonalization, circuit lower bounds) don't apply cleanly across these boundaries — this is called a "complexity barrier."

The one exception we *do* know is strict: `L ⊂ PSPACE` (via the space hierarchy theorem). The middle boundaries — P vs NP especially — remain the deep open questions, which is why P vs NP is a Millennium Prize problem, not routine coursework.
